articles.title: Egypt seeks to expand exports to Africa as intra-African trade reaches $214bn - Daily News Egypt
articles.summary: Egypt seeks to expand exports to Africa as intra-African trade reaches $214bn  Daily News Egypt
articles.full_text:
Egypt is seeking to expand its exports to African markets by diversifying destinations, strengthening commercial partnerships and improving access for Egyptian products, Industry Minister Khaled Hashem said.
Speaking at “Scaling Egypt’s Industrial Champions” forum organised by the American Chamber of Commerce in Egypt (AmCham Egypt) in cooperation with the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), Hashem said Africa offers significant potential for Egyptian exporters, particularly in industrial, agricultural, engineering and building-materials products.
The event, attended by AmCham Egypt Chairman Omar Mehanna, Afreximbank executives and representatives of the business community, brought together government officials, exporters and development finance specialists to discuss ways to expand Egypt’s commercial presence across African markets.
Hashem noted that intra-African trade reached approximately $214bn in 2025, marking an annual increase of 5.5%, while total African merchandise trade stood at around $1.5trn.
Egypt accounted for approximately 4.4% of intra-African trade, equivalent to around $9.3bn, according to figures cited by the minister.
He said the figures demonstrate both the scale of Africa’s existing trade and the room for Egypt to increase its presence in the continent’s markets.
“There is something abnormal about these figures,” Hashem said, referring to Egypt’s share of intra-African trade in relation to its industrial capabilities and production capacity.
He stressed that increasing Egyptian exports to global markets remains a central government objective and a key performance indicator for the industrial sector. Africa, however, offers particularly significant opportunities for rapid export growth, potentially allowing Egyptian exports to multiply over a relatively short period, he added.
Egyptian exports to Africa reach $7.6bn
Trade figures presented at the event highlighted the scale of Egypt’s existing commercial presence in Africa and the opportunities to expand it further.
Egyptian exports to African Union countries reached approximately $7.6bn in 2025, compared with $7.8bn in 2024. Imports from these countries amounted to around $2bn, down from approximately $2.1bn a year earlier.
Total trade between Egypt and African Union countries consequently stood at approximately $9.6bn in 2025, compared with $9.9bn in 2024, according to the detailed figures cited during the discussions.
Egypt’s main exports to African markets include electrical machinery and equipment, plastics, iron and steel, processed food products, fresh vegetables and fruit, as well as salt, stone and cement.
In 2025, exports of electrical machinery and equipment amounted to approximately $633.6m, followed by plastics and plastic products at $544.4m, iron and steel at $528.3m, processed food products at $517.8m, vegetables and fruit at $491.4m, and salt, stone and cement at $446.4m.
Libya was the largest African destination for Egyptian exports, receiving approximately $1.5bn worth of goods in 2025. Algeria followed with $1.2bn, Morocco with $1.1bn, Sudan with $957.1m and Tunisia with $431.3m.
Although North African markets remain major destinations, Hashem stressed the need to strengthen Egypt’s commercial presence in East, West and Central Africa, reducing dependence on a limited number of markets and diversifying export destinations.
Egypt targets new African markets
Hashem said Egypt is pursuing practical investment and trade opportunities across the continent, revealing that another major project in Tanzania would be announced soon.
He also announced plans to visit Côte d’Ivoire in November to discuss and reach agreements on additional major projects, reinforcing Egypt’s economic partnerships with both countries.
“We are serious and taking practical steps at a rapid pace,” he said, calling for the support and participation of all key stakeholders to accelerate implementation and achieve the desired results.
Hashem said Egypt’s efforts to expand its African presence should be supported by closer cooperation between government institutions, financial organisations and private companies.
He also highlighted the importance of ensuring that Egyptian products are able to compete effectively in African markets by meeting required quality and technical standards and by improving the efficiency of trade procedures and transportation networks.
Exporters call for broader African presence
Mohamed Kassem, chairman of the Egyptian Exporters Association, said Africa represents a strategic market for Egyptian businesses, offering considerable opportunities to expand industrial and food exports and improve the competitiveness of locally manufactured products.
He said Egypt’s export performance in Africa does not adequately reflect the strength of its economic relations with the continent, noting that a substantial proportion of Egyptian exports remains concentrated in North African Arab countries and Sudan.
Trade with many other African markets remains relatively limited, he added, highlighting the need for Egyptian companies to expand their presence across the continent.
Kassem pointed to opportunities to increase exports of agricultural products, pharmaceuticals, chemicals and fertilisers, alongside the industrial goods already reaching African markets.
He called for stronger trade facilitation measures, more efficient shipping and logistics networks, improved market intelligence for exporters and greater participation in trade fairs and business missions.
He also stressed the importance of financing and guarantees to help businesses convert export opportunities into actual commercial contracts.
Turning export opportunities into deals
The AmCham Egypt–Afreximbank seminar featured an executive discussion on the practical implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), market access and the expansion of bankable demand.
Participants examined how the agreement could facilitate cross-border commerce, improve access to African markets and mobilise the financing needed to execute export transactions.
The discussions underscored the need for closer coordination between government institutions, financial organisations, business associations and private companies to help exporters identify opportunities and turn them into commercial agreements.
For Egypt, the challenge is not simply to increase the value of exports, but also to establish a stronger and more diversified presence across African markets.
With North African countries currently accounting for a significant share of Egypt’s exports to the continent, expanding into East, West and Central Africa could provide new outlets for Egyptian manufacturers and agricultural producers while broadening the country’s export base.
As Africa’s internal trade continues to grow, Egypt is seeking to use its industrial and production capacity to capture a larger share of the continent’s demand and translate existing economic ties into higher export volumes and new commercial partnerships.

articles.title: EU Extends GSP to 2036, Keeping Duty-Free Access for Tanzanian Exports - TanzaniaInvest
articles.summary: EU Extends GSP to 2036, Keeping Duty-Free Access for Tanzanian Exports  TanzaniaInvest
articles.full_text:
On 26th October 2026, the European Union (EU) confirmed a 10-year extension of its Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP) during an EU–Africa trade press briefing.
The announcement comes as the EU marks 25 years of the Everything But Arms (EBA) scheme and 25 years of formal EU–Africa political relations, which began with the 2000 Cairo Summit.
The extension of the GSP framework means that the EU will be maintaining predictable trade arrangements for developing countries including Tanzania and confirming that the EBA scheme will continue indefinitely for eligible least developed countries (LDCs).
Under the EBA scheme, eligible LDCs will continue to receive automatic, duty-free and quota-free access to the EU market for all products except arms and ammunition, without an expiry date or the need to reapply for the arrangement.
The revised GSP framework will take effect on 1st January 2027 and run for 10 years, through 2036.
Beyond tariff preferences, EU–Africa trade cooperation is increasingly focused on expanding local processing, supporting regional value addition, and strengthening sustainable supply chains.
According to the EU, the Union remains Africa’s largest trade and investment partner as trade in goods between the two partners increased by 51%, from EUR 236 billion in 2016 to EUR 357 billion in 2025. The EU accounts for 33% of Africa’s total trade in goods and is the destination for almost 40% of African exports over the past 25 years.
In 2024, EU companies held more than EUR 250 billion in foreign direct investment stock in Africa, while African investments in the EU exceeded EUR 74 billion and African exports under EBA to the EU increased from EUR 112 million to nearly EUR 5 billion in 2025.
At a national level, Tanzania recorded a 96% utilisation rate for available trade preferences under the scheme, indicating that its exporters are making substantial use of the market access available to eligible products.
Continued EBA access provides an established route for Tanzania into the EU market, the extent to which the country benefits will depend in part on exporters’ ability to use available preferences, meet EU product standards and expand the value of goods produced for export.
Speaking on the matter, the European Commission Spokesperson for Trade, Economic Security and Customs, Olof Gill, stated: “The EU-Africa relationship is a true partnership of equals. Our trade and investment approach is designed to deliver maximum mutual benefit: supporting Africa’s ambitions for sustainable development, industrialisation and jobs, while at the same time helping Europe diversify its partnerships and build resilient supply chains.”
Gill reiterated: “In an increasingly unpredictable geopolitical context, the EU remains Africa’s first trade and investment partner, with longstanding agreements rooted in stability, predictability, and sustainability. 33% of Africa’s total trade in goods is with the EU, which is also the first destination of Africa’s exports, accounting for almost 40%. Both sides benefit from strong trade relations and cooperation. Africa ranks as the EU’s fourth-largest trade partner. Over the past decade, EU trade with Africa has grown by 51%, from EUR 236 billion in 2016 to EUR 357 billion in 2025. Overall, 44 African countries have duty-free access to the EU market, a market of 450 million consumers, and 97% of African exports enter the EU free of import duties.”
“At the same time, compliance with high EU standards opens up other potential markets and makes African products more competitive elsewhere. European investors hold the largest foreign direct investment stock in Africa. In 2024, the investments of EU companies in Africa were worth over EUR 250 billion, while African investments in the EU were worth over EUR 74 billion,” added Gill.
Gill confirmed: “With the 6 Economic Partnership Agreements with 15 countries currently in place, EU’s total trade with African EPA countries increased by 35%, and its foreign direct investment stock in African EPA countries increased from EUR 72 billion in 2014 to EUR 86 billion in 2024. This clearly shows that our Economic Partnership Agreements work and bring tangible benefits to economies on both sides.”
“These Economic Partnership Agreements with six countries in the Southern African Development Community (SADC), Cote d’Ivoire and Ghana were signed 10 years ago and since then our bilateral trade has increased, driving higher value added in the partner countries such as the automotive sector in South Africa or the cocoa sector in West Africa, attracting more investment imports by 61% since 2015,” noted Gill.
The EU’s Generalised Scheme of Preferences (GSP) is a unilateral trade preference scheme that reduces or removes customs duties on eligible goods imported to the EU from developing countries.
It was established in 1971, following international efforts through the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) to help developing countries participate more fully in global trade and it’s current framework entered into force in January 2014.
The EU’s GSP comprises three arrangements: 1) Standard GSP, which provides for the partial or full removal of customs duties on two-thirds of tariff lines for eligible developing countries; 2) GSP+, which offers zero tariffs on these products to eligible vulnerable countries that meet additional requirements; 3) the Everything But Arms (EBA) arrangement, which grants least developed countries duty-free, quota-free access to the EU market for all products except arms and ammunition.

articles.title: Rwanda Mining Board Regains Independence as Mineral Exports Surge - KT PRESS -
articles.summary: Rwanda Mining Board Regains Independence as Mineral Exports Surge  KT PRESS -
articles.full_text:
KIGALI – Rwanda’s Cabinet has approved a new organizational structure that will allow the Rwanda Mines, Petroleum and Gas Board (RMB) to operate as an independent institution, strengthening the regulator’s position.
At its meeting on October 26, the government said the change is intended to strengthen oversight of the mining sector and support its growing contribution to the economy.
In July 2025, RMB was placed under the supervision of the Rwanda Development Board (RDB) as part of a wider institutional review. The latest move points to a significant timing.
Rwanda recorded $1.75 billion in mineral export earnings in 2024, up from about $373 million in 2017, and has set a target of generating $2.17 billion annually from mineral exports by 2029.
As the industry expands, the regulator’s ability to oversee extraction, enforce standards and ensure that mineral resources deliver lasting economic benefits will become increasingly important.
A Regulator with Wide Responsibilities
Beyond issuing mining licenses under the presidential order establishing RMB in 2023, the Board is responsible for regulating and managing mineral, quarry, oil and gas resources, monitoring compliance by license holders.
It is also responsible for conducting geological research as well as overseeing exploration and mineral processing. The board also has powers to inspect operations, impose administrative sanctions for violations and monitor the value-addition and trading of mineral products.
Its responsibilities therefore make it an intersection of investment, resource management, regulatory compliance and the government’s ambition to earn more from its natural resources.
The distinction matters because a growing mining industry requires both investment and credible oversight. Companies need predictable licensing and regulatory processes, while the government must ensure that operators comply with applicable laws and standards.
Rwanda’s position in the global minerals market adds to those demands.
The United States Geological Survey ranked Rwanda the world’s third-largest tantalum producer in 2024, accounting for 15% of global production. The country also ranked sixth in tungsten production and eleventh in tin production.
These minerals are used in electronics and other industrial applications, making Rwanda’s ability to supply international markets responsibly an important part of its export ambitions.
From Mineral Exports to Domestic Processing
Export growth has already changed the scale of Rwanda’s mining landscape. The next step is ensuring that higher earnings translate into greater domestic value addition and a stronger industry.
The government is promoting mechanization, exploration and mineral processing as ways to increase productivity and move beyond dependence on extracting and exporting raw materials.
RMB Chief Executive Officer Alice Uwase has severally championed reforms geared towards increasing export earnings while building more processing capacity within Rwanda and Africa as a whole.
“We are moving toward mechanized extraction, on-site beneficiation, and advanced value addition, with refining facilities for gold, tin, and tantalum already operational in Rwanda,” she said on October 20, 2026 at the Mining in Motion Conference in Accra, Ghana.
Rwanda has established gold refining, tantalum refining and tin-smelting facilities, creating capacity to process minerals locally.
The country’s target of $2.17 billion in annual mineral exports by 2029 will require continued investment and efficient operations. It will also place greater demands on the institutions responsible for oversight of the sector.
RMB’s new institutional status will therefore be judged by what that independence enables it to do. The practical test awaits the new structure to strengthen regulatory capacity while supporting responsible investment and greater value from Rwanda’s mineral resources.
Rwanda Mining Week is scheduled to take place at the Kigali Convention Centre from December 9 to 11 under the theme “Powering the Future: Mechanization, Scale and Sustainable Growth in Mining.”
It is expected to bring together policymakers, investors, mining companies and technology providers. The program includes the launch of Rwanda’s Geoscience Laboratory and Mining Investment Pitchbook.
With the sector pursuing higher export earnings and more sophisticated operations, the decision to give RMB an independent institutional structure sets the stage for renewed attention to how Rwanda regulates its mineral wealth and how effectively that wealth serves the wider economy.

articles.summary: Tanzania Puts Mineral Value Addition at Centre of 2026 Mining Investment Conference  Uchumi360
articles.full_text:

Tanzania will bring more than 3,500 delegates, 500 investors and participants from over 80 countries to Dar es Salaam in November as the government shifts its mining agenda toward domestic processing, critical minerals and mineral based manufacturing. Mining contributed 10.1 percent of GDP in 2024 and mineral exports reached USD5.4 billion in 2025, giving the country a larger resource base from which to pursue value addition.
Tanzania will use the 2026 Tanzania Mining and Investment Conference to make a broader investment case for processing more of its mineral wealth at home, as the government seeks to move the sector beyond extraction and exports toward refining, manufacturing and industrial production. The three day conference will be held from November 19 to 21 at the Julius Nyerere International Convention Centre in Dar es Salaam under the theme, Value Added Minerals: The Engine of Industrial and Economic Growth, bringing together mining companies, mineral processors, investors, financial institutions, technology providers, regulators, researchers and policymakers. President Samia Suluhu Hassan is expected to officiate the opening ceremony, while Zanzibar President Hussein Mwinyi is scheduled to preside over the closing. The programme will cover gold, graphite, rare earths, nickel, mining finance, industrial infrastructure, mineral processing, technology, ESG and the integration of artisanal miners into formal value chains.
The conference comes at a point when mining has already become a much larger part of Tanzania’s economy, which is why the policy conversation is moving from how to increase extraction toward how much more value can be retained after minerals leave the ground. Ministry of Minerals data show that the sector’s contribution to GDP rose from 9.1 percent in 2023 to 10.1 percent in 2024 and continued to strengthen during 2025, while mineral export earnings reached USD5.40 billion in 2025, up from USD4.12 billion in 2024. Gold remained the dominant export, but Tanzania is increasingly trying to position graphite, nickel, rare earths and other critical minerals as the foundation of a broader industrial strategy rather than simply another source of raw commodity exports.
“TMIC 2026 reflects Tanzania’s commitment to transforming its mineral wealth into industrial growth, employment opportunities, technological advancement and sustainable economic prosperity,” Minerals Minister Anthony Mavunde said in the conference material. He added that the government wants investors and industry stakeholders to participate in shaping “the future of mining and mineral value addition in Tanzania and Africa.”
Tanzania Wants Mining to Feed Manufacturing
The central economic argument behind TMIC 2026 is that Tanzania’s mining sector has become large enough for policymakers to focus less narrowly on increasing production and more seriously on the industries that can be built around minerals once they have been extracted. The conference programme identifies value addition opportunities in graphite for battery anodes, nickel and cobalt products, gold bars and jewellery, fertilisers, steel, copper products, cement and ceramics, while also placing industrial parks, special economic zones, smelting, refining and mineral-based manufacturing within the same investment conversation. That represents a significant shift in emphasis because the government is no longer presenting mining simply as an export sector, but as one of the possible foundations of Tanzania’s industrialisation agenda under Vision 2050.
The economics behind that shift are straightforward. Extracting and exporting a mineral captures only a fraction of the total value created before that mineral becomes a finished industrial product. Additional value can be generated through beneficiation, refining, component manufacturing, engineering, logistics, equipment supply, research and industrial services, and those activities generally create more jobs, a larger domestic supplier base and more opportunities for technology transfer than extraction alone. Tanzania’s challenge is therefore not simply to produce more minerals but to determine which parts of the value chain can be developed competitively inside the country and which investments can realistically be supported by domestic power, transport, skills and financing conditions.
Critical Minerals Are Moving to the Centre of the Investment Story
Critical minerals will be one of the most important themes at the conference because Tanzania is trying to position itself within global supply chains that are being reshaped by electric vehicles, battery production, renewable energy and strategic competition over access to raw materials. The country has attracted growing interest because of deposits of graphite, nickel and rare earth elements, including praseodymium and neodymium, which are used in permanent magnets for electric vehicle motors and wind turbines. The programme includes discussions on Tanzania’s place in the global clean energy supply chain, the development of midstream and downstream infrastructure, and the possibility of processing minerals domestically before they enter international markets.
This matters because the global critical minerals debate is increasingly moving beyond questions of where minerals are found toward where they are processed. Major economies including China, the United States, European Union members, Japan and South Korea are competing to secure reliable supply chains, but African producers are trying to avoid a repeat of an older commodity model in which minerals are extracted locally while most downstream value is created elsewhere. Tanzania is explicitly using TMIC 2026 to push a different proposition, one in which critical minerals contribute not only export earnings but also domestic manufacturing, industrial capacity and technology development.
Gold Still Dominates the Sector
Despite the growing attention on critical minerals, gold remains the anchor of Tanzania’s mining economy and still accounts for the overwhelming majority of mineral export earnings. Official figures show gold exports rising sharply in 2025 and continuing to provide most of the country’s foreign exchange income from mining, while other minerals remain much smaller in commercial terms. This concentration explains why the conference programme separates discussions on gold from those on graphite, rare earths and battery metals, because Tanzania is simultaneously managing the sector that already generates substantial revenue and trying to develop the minerals that could define the next phase of investment.
The policy challenge is therefore one of diversification within mining itself. Tanzania has already established itself as a major gold producer, but the next stage requires converting potential in graphite, nickel, rare earths and other minerals into commercially operating projects, and then determining whether those projects can support processing and manufacturing industries locally. That progression is far more difficult than simply attracting exploration capital because it requires larger infrastructure, more sophisticated financing and a much deeper technical base.
Processing Requires Power, Transport and Industrial Infrastructure
The conference concept itself acknowledges that mineral value addition will depend on far more than mining licences or investor interest. Processing plants require reliable electricity, water, industrial land, transport connections, specialised technology and access to sufficiently large markets to justify investment. Smelting, refining and advanced processing can be energy intensive, while downstream manufacturing becomes commercially viable only when power costs, logistics and supply chain reliability are competitive enough to support production at scale.
This places Tanzania’s mining strategy directly inside the country’s wider infrastructure agenda. Reliable electricity will be critical if the country wants to process minerals rather than export concentrates, while railways, roads and ports will determine whether mineral-based industries can move inputs and finished products efficiently. Industrial parks and special economic zones could provide shared infrastructure for processors and manufacturers, but their success will depend on whether they are connected effectively to mines, power supply and export corridors. The value addition debate is therefore not a narrow mining policy issue; it is also a power, logistics, industrial policy and investment coordination issue.
Financing Will Decide How Far the Strategy Can Move
TMIC 2026 will also devote significant attention to financing because downstream mineral investment is considerably more capital intensive than many policymakers acknowledge. Mining projects can already require hundreds of millions or billions of dollars before production begins, and adding processing plants, smelters, industrial zones and manufacturing facilities introduces another layer of technology and market risk. The conference will examine public-private partnerships, development finance, de-risking mechanisms and the question of whether African countries can create financing structures specifically designed for mineral value addition projects.
The commercial case will be decisive. Foreign investors will compare electricity prices, taxation, logistics, labour productivity, regulatory predictability and access to financing before deciding whether to process minerals inside Tanzania or export them to established industrial centres elsewhere. This means value addition cannot rely only on policy directives or export restrictions. articles.title: Ethiopian Ambassador Invites Rawalpindi Business Community To Explore Investment Opportunities - https://greenpost.com.pk/
articles.summary: Ethiopian Ambassador Invites Rawalpindi Business Community To Explore Investment Opportunities  https://greenpost.com.pk/
articles.full_text:
RAWALPINDI, October 27, 2026: Ambassador of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia to Pakistan, H.E. Dr. Oumer H. Oba, has invited the Rawalpindi community to explore investment and trade opportunities in Ethiopia’s growing economy.
The ambassador made the remarks during a comprehensive interactive session with the business community at the Rawalpindi Chamber of Commerce and Industry (RCCI) on Tuesday.
Upon his arrival at the chamber, Dr. Oumer was warmly received by RCCI President Nosherwan Khalil Khan, Senior Vice President Waseem Aslam, Vice President Ikram ur Rehman Abbasi and members of the chamber’s executive body.
The Ethiopian ambassador congratulated the newly elected office-bearers of the RCCI and expressed his best wishes for their successful tenure.
Ethiopia Offers Growing Trade And Investment Potential
Addressing RCCI members, Dr. Oumer described Ethiopia as one of the world’s fastest-growing economies and a strategic gateway to the African continent.
He highlighted Ethiopia’s importance as the host country of the headquarters of the African Union and the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa.
The ambassador said Ethiopia has opened several sectors to foreign investment following the implementation of homegrown economic reforms. He highlighted the country’s industrial parks, affordable and sustainable electricity, regional integration and extensive international air connectivity through Ethiopian Airlines as key advantages for foreign investors.
Business Delegation To Ethiopia Planned
Dr. Oumer also briefed the Rawalpindi business community on a business delegation to Ethiopia being planned by the Ethiopian Embassy in Islamabad.
He invited local entrepreneurs and investors to participate in the initiative and explore opportunities in sectors including agriculture, agro-processing, manufacturing, mining, information and communication technology (ICT) and tourism.
RCCI Seeks Stronger Pakistan-Ethiopia Business Ties
RCCI President Nosherwan Khalil Khan briefed the ambassador on the chamber’s role and the major sectors represented by its business community.
He stressed the need to strengthen trade and investment cooperation between Pakistan and Ethiopia, particularly in pharmaceuticals, surgical goods, textiles and agriculture.
Nosherwan Khalil Khan assured the ambassador of the chamber’s full support in promoting stronger commercial ties between the two countries.
He also expressed the Rawalpindi business community’s keen interest in exploring Ethiopia’s trade and investment potential and developing mutually beneficial business partnerships in the future.
The meeting concluded with a shared commitment to promoting greater interaction between the business communities of Pakistan and Ethiopia and exploring new avenues for bilateral trade and investment.

articles.summary: Ethiopia Earns UN Investment Award With Focus On Safaricom's Digital Expansion  The Reporter Ethiopia
articles.full_text:
The Ethiopian Investment Commission (EIC) has received a United Nations award for its efforts in promoting investment in the digital economy, with Safaricom Ethiopia’s telecommunications infrastructure and the M-PESA mobile money platform cited as key vehicles for advancing digital connectivity and financial inclusion.
The commission was honored with the 2026 UN Investment Promotion Award at the ninth World Investment Forum in Doha, Qatar, according to UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD).
The accolade comes amid a strong upward trend in foreign direct investment. Ethiopia attracted USD 1.432 billion in FDI during the first quarter of the 2026/27 Ethiopian fiscal year, marking a 49 percent increase compared to the same period last year. During the quarter, the EIC issued 179 new investment licenses, while 81 projects entered implementation and 66 commenced production, generating over 22,000 jobs.
UNCTAD commended the commission’s pivotal role in facilitating investment in digital infrastructure. By March 31, 2026, Safaricom Ethiopia expanded its reach to 13.6 million active subscribers and 3,504 network sites, bringing 4G coverage to 59 percent of the population, while M-PESA registered 5.2 million customers.
The EIC’s winning submission was selected from 48 entries representing 40 countries, focusing on initiatives that attract investment into the digital economy. Four other international organizations were also recognized: the Caribbean Export Development Agency for regional investment promotion through the Caribbean Investment Forum; Invest KOREA for driving investments into semiconductor materials, components, and equipment; Invest Qatar for its Startup Qatar initiative; and Morocco’s Tanger Med Zones for investments in digital services, including the ALTEN Delivery Center Maroc.
UNCTAD has presented the Investment Promotion Awards annually since 2002. While the international honor highlights the commission’s effective promotion strategies, Ethiopia’s latest FDI figures offer a concrete measure of the tangible capital flowing into the country’s expanding economy.

articles.title: South Korea Q3 GDP Beats Forecasts Propelled By AI Chip Boom Boosting Exports, Investments - Ventureburn
articles.summary: South Korea Q3 GDP Beats Forecasts Propelled By AI Chip Boom Boosting Exports, Investments  Ventureburn
articles.full_text:
South Korea just announced one of the biggest economic surprises of the year. Its economy grew 1% between July and September. That’s more than 3X what the Bank of Korea (BOK) had projected. The South Korea Q3 GDP figures point to one clear driver: AI chips.
Global hunger for semiconductors kept factories humming, lifted exports, and pulled investment along for the ride. But it’s not all good news. Households are still tightening their belts. And the whole growth story rests on one industry. Here’s what you need to know.
AI Chips Did the Heavy Lifting
Preliminary BOK data shows GDP rose 1% from the previous quarter. Back in August, the central bank expected just 0.3%. Growth also sped up from 0.6% in the second quarter.
Exports did most of the work. They climbed 2.3%, led by semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment. That alone added 1.1 percentage points to growth. Imports rose 2.4% too, partly on chipmaking equipment.
The chip numbers are wild. Semiconductor exports soared 218.7% year-on-year to $148 billion in the quarter, according to government data.
The BOK estimates chips were behind roughly half of all Q3 growth. On a yearly basis, the economy grew 3.4%. That’s a touch slower than the 3.7% seen in the second quarter.
More Updates: Moscow Hosts Russia-Africa Summit and Energy Forum 2026
Investment Follows the Chip Money
When chips sell, chipmakers build. Facility investment jumped 4.1%, mostly on machinery used to make semiconductors. Spending on intellectual property, like R&D and software, rose 2.3%.
Construction picked up 0.7%. Government spending grew 1.9% after officials held back funds earlier in the year. Then there’s income. Real gross domestic income surged 18.8% from a year earlier.
That’s the fastest jump since late 1977. The fuel behind the jump is rising chip prices while oil import costs fall. Simply put, Korea is earning more for what it sells.
More Updates: Bedrock Robotics Raises $600M for Autonomous Heavy Equipment
Consumers Are Still Sitting It Out
Despite all that money, private consumption slipped 0.2%. Two things hurt. A stock market slide since July cut trading volumes and financial services spending. A major automaker strike, the first full-scale one in a decade, also delayed car deliveries.
Without those hits, the BOK says spending would have grown 0.4%. Lee Dong-won, who heads the BOK’s economic statistics department, says corporate profits simply haven’t reached households yet.
He expects that to change. Chipmakers start paying cash dividends this quarter. Performance bonuses land early next year. A stronger won should also cut import prices.
Why This Matters
Growth over the first three quarters already hit 3.6%. That beats the BOK’s full-year forecast of 3.3%. Even zero growth in Q4 keeps the annual figure at 3.6%. If the fourth quarter grows 1.4% or more, Korea could hit 4%.
Per capita income is also nearing a milestone. The finance ministry says it’s almost certain to cross $40,000 this year. That strength cuts both ways for borrowers.
BOK Governor Shin Hyun-song has signalled that core inflation could top forecasts. He wants to keep policy restrictive. So a rate hike before year-end now looks more likely.

By Yinka Kolawole
The Federal Government has launched new trade intelligence tools to help Nigerian businesses access international markets, attract productive investments and strengthen local industries’ competitiveness as part of efforts to build a $1 trillion economy by 2030.
Minister of Industry, Trade and Investment, Dr Jumoke Oduwole, who unveiled the initiative in Abuja, said the tools would provide exporters and investors with reliable market information to guide business decisions, navigate trade requirements and translate economic reforms into industrial growth and job creation.
Oduwole said Nigeria had recorded significant progress in capital inflows and non-oil exports, but stressed the need to convert the gains into productive investments, completed export transactions and stronger domestic industries.
She disclosed that capital importation rose from about $3.9 billion in 2023 to more than $23 billion in 2025, while non-oil exports reached a record N12.36 trillion, with Nigerian products gaining access to more than 120 countries.

articles.full_text:
HARARE – A $250,000 car announced as a gift by the late tenderpreneur Wicknell Chivayo and rejected by lawyer Lewis Uriri may have been fraudulently imported, with documents suggesting the transaction was processed in Uriri’s name without his knowledge, ZimLive can reveal.
Documents seen by ZimLive show that the vehicle was bought from Johannesburg dealer Verve Auto Sports and cleared by the Zimbabwe Revenue Authority (ZIMRA) in Uriri’s name, using an uncertified copy of his passport.
The vehicle was subsequently delivered to Exquisite Motors in Harare, before Chivayo announced on X on September 21 – nine days before his death in a helicopter crash near Marondera – that he was gifting it to Uriri in recognition of legal services provided over the years.
Uriri rejected both the vehicle and a $50,000 cash gift described as being “for fuel”, telling Chivayo that the announcement “came as a complete surprise, without prior notice or discussion”.
Uriri, who is part of a legal team representing activists challenging constitutional amendments that extended President Emmerson Mnangagwa’s term, said relations between the two men had been strained for years.
He said he considered it “necessary to decline benefits that could reasonably create a perception of personal financial obligation extending beyond a concluded and fully remunerated professional engagement”.
Chivayo subsequently offered the same vehicle to another lawyer, Advocate Silvester Hashiti, this time with an additional $500,000 cash gift. But Chivayo died before Hashiti could collect the vehicle. Exquisite Motors has reportedly referred Hashiti to the executor of Chivayo’s estate.
The documents show that the car was purchased for R2,882,782, with ZIMRA collecting US$74,460.57 in import duty.
As part of the customs clearance process, the importer’s identity must be established. ZimLive understands that Chivayo supplied an uncertified copy of Uriri’s old passport, which was attached to the import documentation.
Chivayo may have retained the copy from earlier dealings with Uriri, who had travelled outside Zimbabwe in connection with his legal work.
But the passport had been cancelled in 2024 after running out of pages. Uriri subsequently obtained a new passport, a copy of which was seen by our correspondent.
A cancelled passport is no longer valid identification for establishing the holder’s current identity in a transaction of this nature. More significantly, legal experts say the documents raise questions about whether the importation was falsely presented as an act undertaken by Uriri.
Advocate Thabani Mpofu, who was shown the documents, said the transaction may have breached the law.
“You have a document that says Advocate Uriri imported a vehicle into the country. That document tells a lie about its own contents. The transfer (to settle customs duty) that is presented in Uriri’s name is false and fraudulent,” Mpofu said.
“Wicknell ought to have imported the vehicle in his name and thereafter lawfully donated it to Uriri. Upon acceptance of the donation, Uriri would then have taken title.”
Mpofu said that by presenting the transaction as Uriri’s, Chivayo and the ZIMRA officials who approved the clearance may have committed “fraud against the due administration of justice.”
“The vehicle was imported fraudulently, is the subject of the commission of criminal misconduct and must therefore be forfeited to the state,” Mpofu argued.
DOWNLOAD URIRI CAR IMPORT DOCUMENTS
ZIMRA spokesman Gladman Njani declined to comment on the specific transaction, citing statutory confidentiality obligations.
“ZIMRA is bound by confidentiality obligations under the Revenue Authority Act [Chapter 23:11] and the Customs and Excise Act [Chapter 23:02]. These laws restrict the disclosure of information obtained in the course of official duties, except as permitted by law. Accordingly, ZIMRA cannot comment on the tax or customs affairs of specific individuals or entities,” Njani said.
“ZIMRA remains committed to the lawful and consistent administration of customs requirements, maintaining the integrity of its processes and safeguarding confidential information.”
Exquisite Motors owner Victor Vikela said his company had merely stored the vehicle at Chivayo’s request.
“We had nothing whatsoever to do with its acquisition and importation,” Vikela said.
Vikela confirmed that the vehicle was no longer at the showroom but declined to disclose where it had been moved.
Uriri declined to discuss the matter further.
“You guys must just let Wicknell rest in peace,” he said.

Photo: Contributed
By: Peneyambeko Jonas
Namibia must strengthen local production, processing and export capacity to benefit from China’s zero-tariff policy, speakers at the China-Africa Cooperation Symposium said in Windhoek on Tuesday.
The symposium, held at the Hilton Hotel under the theme China-Africa Partnership at 70: Deepening Collaboration and Exchanges.
It brought together government officials, economists, researchers and business representatives to discuss trade opportunities and ways to increase economic benefits from cooperation with China.
Minister of International Relations and Trade Selma Ashipala-Musavyi said China’s zero-tariff initiative, effective from 1 May 2026 to 30 April 2028 for 20 additional African countries, including Namibia, creates opportunities for export diversification, investment and job creation.
However, she cautioned that tariff-free access alone would not guarantee increased exports.
“However, tariff-free access must be matched by overcoming non-tariff barriers,” she said, referring to requirements such as rules of origin, quality, packaging and phytosanitary standards.
She said Namibia should use the initiative to expand exports beyond traditional products and attract investment into manufacturing, agro-processing, green energy and mineral beneficiation.
The minister pointed to a phytosanitary protocol signed in July 2026 allowing Namibian table grapes to be exported to China as an example of how diplomatic agreements can create market opportunities.
She said similar opportunities should be pursued for processed foods, meat and fisheries.
Chairperson of the Economic Association of Namibia, Jason Kasuto, said the main challenge was whether local businesses could produce goods in sufficient quantities and meet the requirements of Chinese buyers.
“A tariff set to zero is an invitation, and an invitation is only as valuable as the guest’s ability to accept it,” he said.
Kasuto said many Namibian businesses lacked the production scale, certification, working capital and logistics needed to supply the Chinese market consistently.
He argued that Namibia should negotiate for more local processing of minerals, skills transfer, measurable local-content requirements and Namibian participation in ownership.
He also called for clear mining policies and disciplined public finances to ensure that investment in minerals and petroleum creates lasting economic benefits.
Economist Emmanuel Matambo of the Centre for Africa-China Studies said the zero-tariff initiative could help African countries increase exports to China and reduce trade imbalances.
He said Africa-China trade reached US$348 billion in 2025, with African exports accounting for US$123 billion and Chinese exports reaching US$225 billion, leaving Africa with a trade deficit of US$102 billion.
Matambo said African countries needed to diversify their exports, including through agriculture and value-added products, rather than relying mainly on raw materials.
Meanwhile, University of Botswana political scientist Stanley Ehiane said African countries should play a stronger role in determining the terms and outcomes of their economic partnerships with China.
He called for African governments to negotiate collectively through institutions such as the African Union, the Southern African Development Community and the African Continental Free Trade Area.
Ehiane also urged governments to make technology transfer, skills development, transparent agreements and debt management central to cooperation.
He said civil society, universities, trade unions, local communities and the media should participate in decisions involving major investment projects.
The speakers agreed that Namibia’s access to China’s market must be supported by stronger local industries, export-ready businesses and regional cooperation.
For Namibia, the economic test will be whether the policy increases local production, creates jobs and enables businesses to earn more from goods produced within the country.

By Nkiruka Nnorom
Nigeria and South Africa have emerged among the leading drivers of Russia-Africa’s trade which exceeded $27 billion in 2025, even as Moscow outlined five- point strategic plans to deepen economic ties with the continent.
Director, Information and Press Department and Spokesperson, Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Russian Federation, Maria Zakharova, disclosed this at the Russia-Africa Media Forum ahead of the third Russia-Africa Summit billed for October 28 and 29 in Moscow.
Zakharova said Russia’s largest trading partners traditionally were Egypt and Algeria, while economic ties were actively developing with other African states, including Nigeria, Morocco, South Africa, and Tunisia, among others.
“Following the results of 2025 of last year, the trade turnover of Russia with the countries of Africa exceeded $27 billion.
“Our largest trading partners traditionally are Egypt, and Algeria, economic ties are actively developing with Morocco, South Africa, Tunisia, Nigeria, other states.”
Zakharova stressed that Russia’s support for Africa’s independent role goes beyond rhetoric, citing five priority directions, including support for sovereignty and independence through security, food and energy; assistance in settling armed conflicts under the principle “African problems – African solution”; deepening interaction within the African Union and Russia-Africa Partnership Forum, as well as increasing trade with Africa Continental Free Trade Area, AfCFTA, and Afreximbank, and humanitarian ties.
She said food security remained central to Moscow’s partnership with Africa, noting that over 18 million tons of grain were delivered to Africa in 2025, while 13 million tons have been delivered in first nine months of 2026. She added that fertilizer supplies rose from 1.5 million tons to over 2.2 million tons within the same period.
“One of the most important directions for us and for Russia, and for the African continent remains, is and will be ensuring food security,” she said, adding that “only for the past year Russia delivered to African countries over 18 million tons of grain, and for the first 9 months of the current year delivered another 13 million tons.”
She added that fertilizer deliveries grew from 1.5 million tons last year to over 2.2 million tons this year.
Responding to a question on what political place Africa should occupy in the new world order, she said Russia’s position was clearly stated in its Foreign Policy Concept approved on March 31, 2023.
Quoting Chapter 57 of the document, she said: “Russia is in solidarity with African states in their aspiration toward the establishment of a fairer multipolar world and the elimination of socio-economic inequality, which is amplified due to the sophisticated neo-colonial policy of a number of developed states regarding Africa.”
According to her, “The Russian Federation intends to facilitate the further establishment of Africa as a distinctive and influential center of world development.”
“We view African states as independent, equal partners with whom we are connected by long-standing traditions of friendship and cooperation,” she said.
Recalling historical ties, she said Soviet specialists built about 30 energy facilities, three oil refineries, 29 machine-building enterprises and about 100 educational institutions, while 480,000 Africans were trained. Over 40,000 African students currently study in Russia.
On media, she said: “Russian information broadcasting covers more than 40 states of the African continent. Moreover we speak not only about the dissemination of Russian news, we speak precisely about joint journalistic work.”
On diplomatic presence, she said: “Today in Africa 48 Russian embassies operate. Since 2022 three new diplomatic representations were opened: in South Sudan, in Gambia, in the Union of the Comoros.”
She said five more resumed work in Burkina Faso, Equatorial Guinea, Niger, Sierra Leone and Togo, with the 49th planned in Liberia, while 22 bilateral intergovernmental commissions are working.
“This is a very important tool; intergovernmental commissions unite ministers, vice-premiers, this gives the opportunity immediately, literally from the wheels to solve questions,” she said.
She said the summit will focus on trade, investments, food security, energy, digital technologies, artificial intelligence and creation of independent payment systems, with over 2,000 participants expected.

JOHANNESBURG, 27 October 2026: The Retail Motor Industry Organisation (RMI) has welcomed the recognition of South Africa’s automotive aftermarket as a significant contributor to the economy, following the opening address by Deputy Minister of Trade Industry and Competition, John Steenhuisen, at the CEO Breakfast at Automechanika Johannesburg 2026 at Gallagher Convention Centre today.
Addressing industry leaders, exhibitors and business representatives, Steenhuisen highlighted the aftermarket’s substantial economic contribution, noting that the retail and aftermarket economy traded approximately R933 billion in 2025, contributed R202.6 billion to GDP and supported more than 310,000 jobs – around 70% of total automotive employment. The sector encompasses more than 23,000 businesses, the overwhelming majority of which are small and medium-sized enterprises. He also highlighted its potential to drive localisation, job creation, exports and technical skills development.
These figures underscore the aftermarket’s central role in South Africa’s economic resilience, industrial capability and mobility, with opportunities to build on this contribution through greater localisation and regional trade.
Steenhuisen’s address reinforced the importance of looking beyond new vehicle manufacturing to recognise the extensive network of businesses that keep South Africa’s approximately 13 million vehicles safe, roadworthy and operational throughout their lifecycles.
“If manufacturing is the birth of the vehicle, the aftermarket is the life of the vehicle,” Steenhuisen said, underscoring the essential role played by businesses that service, repair, test, maintain and supply parts for the country’s vehicle fleet.
Henk Ferreira, Chief Operating Officer (COO) of the RMI, welcomed the recognition of the sector’s contribution to South Africa’s broader automotive value chain.
“The aftermarket supports hundreds of thousands of jobs and thousands of businesses, many of them small and medium-sized enterprises. It provides essential services to motorists and businesses while sustaining technical expertise and economic activity across the country.
“We welcome the Deputy Minister’s recognition that the automotive industry’s potential extends well beyond the production line. South Africa’s existing vehicle fleet represents significant ongoing demand for replacement parts, maintenance and repair services, creating opportunities to retain more value locally and strengthen the broader automotive value chain.”
Localisation beyond the factory gate
A key theme of Steenhuisen’s address was the opportunity to expand local production of replacement parts and reduce reliance on imports. He noted that South Africa imported approximately R107.5 billion worth of replacement parts in 2025, while around 76% of vehicles on the country’s roads are outside their warranty period.
“In practical terms, this means the majority of vehicle maintenance and repair activity has already shifted beyond the original manufacturer ecosystem and into the broader aftermarket,” he said.
“The opportunity, therefore, is not limited to the roughly 600,000 vehicles produced annually. The opportunity lies in the 13 million vehicles already on our roads.”
The Deputy Minister said the review of the Automotive Production and Development Programme (APDP2) should consider the broader automotive ecosystem, including the businesses that maintain and repair vehicles throughout their useful lives.
“Localisation must extend beyond the factory gate to include the businesses that keep South Africans moving every day,” he said.
Expanding opportunities beyond our borders
Steenhuisen identified the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) as another significant opportunity for industrial growth, pointing to growing demand across Southern Africa for affordable replacement parts, remanufactured components, technical expertise and aftermarket services.
South Africa, he said, was well positioned to build on its established engineering capability, distribution networks and technical expertise to expand its role in regional automotive value chains.
“The export opportunity is therefore no longer confined to complete vehicles and original equipment components. It also includes replacement parts, remanufactured products, vehicle maintenance expertise and specialised services,” he said.
“By strengthening our aftermarket capabilities and supporting localisation, we can position South Africa not only as a manufacturing hub, but also as the leading automotive services and aftermarket hub for the African continent.”
Skills development critical to future competitiveness
The Deputy Minister emphasised that the transition towards electric and hybrid vehicles, advanced driver-assistance systems and increasingly sophisticated diagnostic technologies requires sustained investment in people and technical capability.
While apprenticeship numbers have increased, he noted that South Africa has approximately 31% fewer qualified automotive artisans than in 2009.
“The goal is not simply training more people. It is building deeper technical capability,” he said.
Ferreira agreed that developing future-ready skills was essential to the industry’s ability to adapt.
“Technology is changing the way vehicles are serviced, diagnosed and repaired. Our skills pipeline must keep pace, ensuring that technicians and artisans have the competencies required to work safely and effectively on increasingly complex vehicles.”
He said the RMI welcomed continued collaboration between industry, government, merSETA, TVET colleges and training providers to strengthen apprenticeship pathways, workplace learning and specialised technical training. This would help give young people access to meaningful careers while building the capability the industry needs.
Road safety and sustainability
Steenhuisen also highlighted the aftermarket’s contribution to road safety, pointing to the importance of vehicle maintenance, quality repairs, roadworthiness testing and appropriate standards in reducing risks on South Africa’s roads.
“Proper maintenance is not only good business. It is a public good,” he said, noting that policy, enforcement, maintenance standards, testing and industry collaboration could make a measurable difference.
He also recognised the role of vehicle repair and remanufacturing in supporting a circular economy. Extending the useful life of vehicles preserves value, reduces waste and avoids unnecessary replacement costs, while effective end-of-life vehicle management will become increasingly important as international environmental expectations evolve.
Turning opportunity into action
Concluding his address, Steenhuisen called for a stronger focus on implementation, highlighting the aftermarket’s potential to advance localisation, support small businesses, create jobs, improve road safety, develop scarce skills and expand regional trade.
“What makes me optimistic is that the automotive aftermarket does not require us to start from scratch,” he said. “The businesses already exist. The skills pipeline already exists. The customer base already exists. The demand already exists. The infrastructure is already here.”
Ferreira welcomed the emphasis on practical implementation and sustained collaboration between government and industry.
“The opportunity is to build on the capabilities already within our sector, creating the conditions for businesses to grow, innovate and compete while delivering benefits for motorists, workers and the wider economy,” he said.
In closing, Steenhuisen thanked the RMI, Messe Frankfurt, industry associations, exhibitors and businesses for their contribution to the economy.
“You are not simply servicing vehicles. You are supporting mobility. You are supporting trade. You are supporting livelihoods. And you are helping build a more competitive and resilient South African economy.
“Let us continue working together to ensure that the automotive industry does not only manufacture vehicles for Africa, but services, maintains, innovates and creates value for Africa throughout the entire life of those vehicles,” Steenhuisen concluded.

Africa’s gas opportunity extends beyond LNG exports
AFRICA: AFRICA is approaching a pivotal moment in its gas industry. The next phase of growth will depend not only on exporting liquefied natural gas (LNG) to global markets, but also on using gas to generate electricity, power industries, expand trade and strengthen energy security across the continent.
The opportunity is considerable. Gas accounts for about 25 per cent of global primary energy supply, compared with just 17 per cent in sub-Saharan Africa, excluding North Africa, according to the Energy Institute’s Statistical Review of World Energy.
After years of uneven progress, the region is positioning itself for a significant expansion of gas production and consumption. The prospects will be a key focus of discussions at Africa Energy Week 2026. Yet the timing presents both an opportunity and a challenge.
A major wave of new LNG capacity is expected to enter the global market over the coming years, led by the United States but with African producers, particularly Mozambique, also preparing to expand.
The International Energy Agency expects more than 330 billion cubic metres a year of additional global LNG export capacity to come online between 2025 and 2030 from projects already under construction at the start of 2025.
The scale of this expansion could reshape global supply and pricing, although project delays and geopolitical disruptions may alter the outlook.
For African producers, the challenge will be to secure markets, attract investment and ensure that new projects deliver benefits beyond export earnings. At the same time, disruptions to oil and LNG supplies through the Strait of Hormuz have highlighted the risks of relying on concentrated energy supply routes.
Diversifying production geographically and reducing exposure to geopolitical chokepoints have consequently become more important to energy-importing countries. Sub-Saharan Africa has an opportunity to contribute to that diversification.
Nigeria and Mozambique are particularly well positioned to supply international markets, while emerging importers such as South Africa, Kenya, Côte d’Ivoire and Namibia could create additional demand.
Three countries shaping Africa’s gas expansion
Three countries illustrate the different ways in which gas could reshape the region’s energy landscape: Côte d’Ivoire through domestic power generation, Nigeria through the expansion of production and LNG exports, and Mozambique through largescale export infrastructure and regional energy integration.
Côte d’Ivoire: linking gas to electricity demand
Côte d’Ivoire stands out because it already has an established gasto-power sector. The country’s experience offers a potential model for economies seeking to use domestic gas to meet growing electricity demand. Eni has advanced its Baleine oil and gas development through successive phases, with a third phase planned.
The project produces oil alongside associated gas, strengthening the potential contribution of domestic resources to the energy system. Rapidly rising electricity demand is also creating pressure to secure reliable gas supplies.
Agreements with Exmar for a floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) arrangement point to the role imported LNG could play in complementing domestic production.
Côte d’Ivoire could therefore provide a useful model for combining domestic gas production, imported LNG and power generation to support economic growth.
Nigeria: expanding production while serving domestic consumers
Nigeria’s federally backed Decade of Gas initiative has gained momentum since 2023, supported by policy and fiscal measures intended to encourage investment and raise production. Several gas projects have reached final investment decisions, with further developments expected as the country seeks to expand supply for both exports and domestic consumption.
Nigeria LNG’s planned expansion towards 30 million tonnes per annum of capacity from 2027 is part of a broader effort to increase export earnings. At the same time, the country is targeting domestic gas production of 12 billion cubic feet per day by 2030.
Meeting both ambitions will require investment across the gas value chain, from production and processing to pipelines, power generation and industrial distribution. Nigeria could demonstrate how a major gas-producing economy can expand LNG exports while increasing supplies for domestic industries and smaller-scale LNG markets.
Mozambique: building a major LNG export hub
Mozambique is emerging as one of Africa’s most consequential gas investment destinations after years of delays associated with insecurity in the north of the country. Coral South, which began production in 2022, has established Mozambique as an LNG exporter.
Further expansion is under way or planned. Eni’s Coral North floating LNG project reached a final investment decision in October 2025, while construction on TotalEnergies’ Mozambique LNG project resumed in January 2026 after the lifting of force majeure.
The projects are expected to add substantial export capacity as they progress towards production. The proposed 18.6-milliontonne-per-annum Rovuma LNG development represents another major opportunity.
Its partners have been advancing preparations towards a final investment decision targeted for 2026, although the investment decision and the required approvals remain critical milestones. Together, these developments could establish Mozambique as a major global LNG supplier over the next decade.
But its potential extends beyond exports. Domestic gas could support electricity generation, industrial development and smaller-scale LNG distribution to neighbouring countries.
Pipeline supplies and regional power links could also help expand access to energy across southern and eastern Africa. With the right infrastructure, financing and regional agreements, Mozambique could become an important anchor for energy integration in the region.
Markets to watch
Beyond these leading producers, several countries face decisions that could shape their energy systems well into the 2030s. Ghana is seeking to strengthen its gas infrastructure as industrial demand grows. Planned pipeline developments and the potential entry of LNG imports through Tema could provide additional supply options, although the timing and commercial viability of new infrastructure will be decisive.
Namibia has attracted significant attention following major offshore oil discoveries in the Orange Basin. Gas development is more complicated because some associated gas may initially be reinjected to support oil production. A comprehensive gas master plan will be needed to determine how commercially recoverable gas can eventually support domestic energy and industry.
South Africa faces two interconnected challenges: developing gas-fired power generation and securing the LNG infrastructure needed to supply it. Additional gas-to-power capacity has been proposed as part of efforts to strengthen electricity supply.
But projects will depend on the availability and affordability of gas, the development of import terminals and pipelines, and the ability to secure reliable long-term supplies. South Africa must also consider the potential of its own offshore resources, including the Orange Basin, while recognising that exploration success does not automatically translate into commercially available gas.
Tanzania presents a particularly important case of the gap between resource potential and commercial development. The country began producing natural gas in 2004 and discovered substantial offshore resources from 2010 onwards.
The project’s progress towards a Host Government Agreement and the subsequent investment decision will be central to determining when Tanzania can begin exploiting its offshore resources on a large scale. The opportunity extends beyond LNG exports.
Tanzania could use gas to expand electricity generation, supply industries, support fertiliser production and develop compressed natural gas and smaller-scale LNG markets. But capturing these benefits will require commercial agreements, infrastructure investment, clear implementation timelines and a domestic market capable of absorbing additional production.
Turning domestic gas into economic growth
A further opportunity lies in converting gas already produced onshore into usable energy rather than treating it primarily as an upstream commodity. Compressed natural gas (CNG), small-scale LNG (SSLNG) and gas-to-power projects can connect gas resources to transport, businesses, industries and electricity consumers.
These options may be particularly relevant in markets where large export terminals are not commercially viable or where demand is dispersed across several locations. Countries including Botswana, Namibia, Nigeria, South Africa and Zimbabwe are exploring different approaches to using gas for domestic energy and industrial development.
The economics will vary from market to market. Projects need dependable supply, sufficient demand, appropriate infrastructure and financing structures that can support investment over the long term. Regional cooperation could also open markets that would be difficult to serve individually.
Smaller economies, including Lesotho, Eswatini, Mauritius and Zambia, may benefit from cross-border electricity trade or smaller-scale gas supply arrangements where the infrastructure and commercial case are viable. Uganda, meanwhile, could explore the use of associated gas to meet some of the energy requirements of its emerging oil industry.
These possibilities underline a broader point: Africa’s gas opportunity is not confined to the countries with the largest reserves. It also involves building the infrastructure and commercial relationships needed to connect producers with consumers.

South Korea's economy expanded at more than triple the expected pace in the third quarter, fueled by strong semiconductor demand, central bank data showed Tuesday.
The country's gross domestic product (GDP) grew 1.0% in the July-September period compared to the previous three months, according to preliminary figures from the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The figure exceeded the central bank's forecast of 0.3% growth made in August.
Growth was supported by a 2.3% rise in exports, "led by semiconductors, machinery and electrical equipment," the BOK said.
Investment in facilities also jumped 4.1%, driven mainly by machinery used in semiconductor manufacturing.
From a year earlier, the country's economy expanded 3.4%, slightly below the 3.7% recorded in the previous quarter.
The country's real gross domestic income (GDI), a measure of purchasing power, surged 18.8% year-over-year, its fastest increase in nearly 49 years, helped by rising semiconductor prices.
South Korea's economy recorded its fastest growth in over five years in the January-March period, expanding 1.7% from the previous three months owing to soaring semiconductor demand.
The semiconductor boom has also propelled the country's current account surplus to record levels.
The country recorded a $116.6 billion current account surplus in the second quarter, surpassing the combined surpluses of manufacturing powerhouses Germany and Japan for the first time since comparable records began in 1996.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts South Korea's annual current account surplus will reach $421.9 billion this year, the second-largest among 190 economies after China.
Semiconductor exports surged 218.7% year-over-year to $148 billion in the third quarter, according to government data.
